summary:
Israeli voters are coalition-minded, but coalition signals mostly move votes inside a bloc rather than adding votes to it. Cross-national work finds coalition-directed voting is common (D10-F01). Israeli studies already on file show coalition considerations decide about 1 vote in 10 (P-F27), that the effect is concentrated among mainstream-party voters (D1-F24), and that in 2019-20 voters switched toward their preferred formateur (D1-F25). Experiments add four points. Explicit signals raise the weight voters give to coalitions relative to parties (D10-F04). Uncertainty about a party's coalition prospects lowers its support even when the expected payoff is the same (D10-F05). Signals change where voters place a party ideologically, much more so for a new party (D10-F06). Only a small minority actually votes strategically (D10-F03). For the change bloc, naming one PM candidate and one main path to government will shift votes toward the lead list and reduce what ambiguity costs, but it will add few seats to the bloc. For Yashar, a new party, every coalition statement also tells voters where it stands.

The arithmetic is the binding constraint. The forecast gives the four change lists about 51 seats. P(change alone >=61) is about 5%, and it rises to about 19% with Ra'am (D10-F32). Any change-led government therefore needs at least one of three things: Ra'am inside or as written outside support, a haredi party, or Likud without Netanyahu. If the bloc gives absolute pre-election pledges against all three, it limits itself to the 5% branch and makes a broken pledge likely. Voters punish parties they see as compromising (D10-F14). Junior partners lose votes (D10-F13). In 2020-22 the pledge-breakers paid the price: Gantz's party fell to 8 seats, and Yamina's remnant, Shaked's Jewish Home, won 1.2% and missed the threshold (D10-F25, D10-F26).

Formation follows Basic Law: The Government (D10-F16). The first mandate is assigned within 7 days of the results and runs 28+14 days. A second MK then gets 28 days, and after that there is a 21-day window for a Knesset majority to name a candidate. If all of that fails, the Knesset dissolves and the election falls on the last Tuesday before day 90, which puts a rerun between mid-April and mid-May 2027. The President has no statutory criteria and follows recommendations, not list size (D10-F17). If Shas and UTJ recommend nobody, as Maariv/JPost report they may (D10-F29), Netanyahu would have about 39-43 recommendations against about 51 for a single change candidate. That makes the first mandate, and the bargaining bonus that goes with it (D10-F10), winnable, but only if all four lists name the same person. In 2019 President Rivlin reportedly counted it against Gantz that 10 of his 54 recommenders would not sit in his government (D10-F18).

A minority government is legally cheap to form. Investiture needs only a simple majority of those voting (60-59-1 in 2021), and removing a government needs 61 votes for a named alternative (D10-F20, D10-F21). The real tests are passing the budget within 145 days and keeping outside supporters on board. Minority cabinets with written support agreements last about as long as majority cabinets; those without such agreements are much more likely to fall early (D10-F12). Rabin's 1993-95 government survived on outside Arab votes (D10-F23). Rotation is now enforceable in law: the PM cannot fire the alternate's ministers, and a dissolution engineered from the PM's side, or a failed budget, hands office to the alternate (D10-F19). That makes rotation offers credible, whether Eisenkot-Bennett or a unity deal with a post-Netanyahu Likud. Haredi parties have joined non-Likud governments only when they were pivotal and the right had no path (D10-F28).

Implications for the next 14 days:
1. Name one PM candidate and publish a rotation and portfolio framework.
2. Make the Arab-party line conditional, policy-based and non-delegitimising (a leadership decision; see D1-F33 and D5-F04).
3. Present the draft as a policy test, not a ban on parties.
4. State openness to governing with Likud after Netanyahu, which undecided voters favour (D5-F22).
5. Prepare a unified recommendation, draft coalition and support agreements, and a 145-day budget plan.
6. Keep supporter lists and field teams in place for a spring-2027 rerun, which the forecast puts at about 42%.

findings.topic: Coalition-directed voting is common (cross-national)
findings.claim: Voters anticipate the policy bargains that potential coalition partners will strike after the election, and these expectations shape their vote. In data from 86 voter-preference surveys across 23 countries over more than 25 years, coalition-directed voting occurs with considerable frequency wherever multiparty coalition governments are the norm. This is the comparative foundation for the Israeli findings already on file (P-F26, P-F27, D1-F24, D1-F25).
findings.quant: 86 surveys, 23 countries, more than 25 years. The abstract reports frequency qualitatively ('considerable'); no pooled share was retrieved.
findings.authors: Raymond M. Duch; Jeff May; David A. Armstrong
findings.title: Coalition-directed Voting in Multiparty Democracies
findings.relevance: Israel is a pure coalition system, so many voters judge parties by the government they make likely. Change-bloc messaging that leaves the likely coalition undefined gives up a lever that voters actually use.

findings.topic: Strategic coalition voting: three mechanisms, conditional on uncertainty (Austria)
findings.claim: A survey before Austria's 2006 election supports three kinds of strategic coalition voting. Big-party supporters lend 'rental' votes to a junior partner at risk of missing the 4% threshold; small-party supporters avoid wasting votes on a list unlikely to pass; and some voters back a larger partner to shape the next coalition's make-up or portfolios. Each effect depends on a voter both preferring the coalition and being uncertain whether it will win a majority. Supporters of the two big parties cast the fewest insincere votes, and the parties themselves sent few, mixed coalition signals.
findings.quant: n = 1,501 national sample plus 450 in Carinthia; fieldwork 18-30 Sept 2006; 11-point party and coalition ratings and 4-point certainty scales. Effects are shown as interaction plots (no single pooled pp).
findings.title: Strategic coalition voting: Evidence from Austria
findings.relevance: In 2026 the change bloc's majority is very uncertain, which is exactly the condition under which coalition-minded voters act. All four change lists poll well above 3.25%, so rental votes are not needed inside the bloc. The live mechanisms are wasted-vote avoidance (Blue and White, Reservists; see P-F24, P-F25) and composition voting toward the list expected to lead.

findings.topic: Polls and coalition signals: perceptions vs actual strategic voting (experiment)
findings.claim: In a laboratory experiment run during two real election campaigns, the authors manipulated polls and coalition signals. Voters who actively sought information formed fairly accurate expectations of the outcome, which made up for lower political sophistication. Strategic voting in the strict sense was confirmed for only a small number of voters. Most insincere vote choices had other explanations, so counting every insincere voter as strategic overstates the effect.
findings.quant: Experimental manipulation of polls and coalition signals; strategic voting is supported 'only for a small number of voters' (abstract).
findings.title: Polls, coalition signals and strategic voting: An experimental investigation of perceptions and effects
findings.relevance: Sets an upper bound. Coalition messaging moves a small slice of voters, consistent with the roughly 1 in 10 coalition-motivated votes in Israel (P-F27). Plan for seat-level effects inside the bloc, not bloc-level swings.

findings.topic: Coalition signals raise the weight of coalition considerations
findings.claim: The authors model the vote as a weighted mix of party and coalition considerations and test it with survey experiments in two countries. Explicit signals about desirable and undesirable coalitions increase the weight voters put on coalition considerations and reduce the weight on party considerations, and some voters change their vote intention as a result.
findings.quant: Survey experiments in two countries; the direction is consistent across both. Magnitudes were not retrieved (abstract only).
findings.authors: Thomas Gschwend; Michael F. Meffert; Lukas F. Stoetzer
findings.title: Weighting Parties and Coalitions: How Coalition Signals Influence Voting Behavior
findings.relevance: A clear signal works best where the coalition being signalled is more popular with target voters than the party sending it. A popular signal, such as 'a Zionist unity government after Netanyahu', can lift a party. An unpopular one, such as Ra'am inside the government for soft-right voters (D1-F33), pulls coalition considerations to the front exactly where they hurt.

findings.topic: Coalition uncertainty itself costs votes (risk aversion)
findings.claim: Observational analyses of several national election studies show that when voters see a party's coalition prospects as uncertain, they are less likely to vote for it, even holding the expected payoff of the possible governments constant. A survey vignette experiment confirms this causally: uncertain coalition prospects reduce support compared with certain prospects that have the same expected payoff. Voters behave as if they are risk-averse about coalitions.
findings.quant: Observational multi-study analysis plus a vignette experiment. Effect sizes were not retrieved (abstract and publisher notice only).
findings.authors: Oke Bahnsen; Lukas F. Stoetzer; Thomas Gschwend
findings.title: Coalition-Directed Voting Under Uncertainty
findings.venue: The Journal of Politics (accepted April 2025; online)
findings.relevance: 'We will decide after the election' carries an electoral price. The change bloc should reduce uncertainty about who leads and the main path to government, while keeping fallbacks conditional rather than unstated.

findings.topic: Coalition signals reposition a party, especially a new one
findings.claim: During Valencia's May 2015 regional campaign, an online survey experiment randomly varied the coalition signals of an established party (PSOE) and a new one (Ciudadanos): rule out all coalitions, a partner to the right, a partner to the left, or a placebo. The signals shifted where respondents placed both parties on the left-right scale. For the new party only, they also changed its image for honesty and office-seeking and respondents' stated probability of voting for it, while the established party's image barely moved.
findings.quant: N = 1,000 (Netquest panel, 12-18 May 2015), 7 arms (about 143 per arm). Manipulation check: a Cs-PP signal raised the share expecting a Cs-PP coalition from 60.3% (placebo) to 85.0%. Effects are larger for the new party.
findings.title: Show Me Your Friends: A Survey Experiment on the Effect of Coalition Signals
findings.relevance: Yashar is a new list whose ideological image is still forming. Signalling unity with a post-Netanyahu Likud will move it right in voters' eyes, which helps with soft-Likud and masorti voters and risks some centre-left voters moving to Democrats or Together (an intra-bloc move). Signalling Ra'am will move it left. Choose deliberately which audience each signal is for.

findings.topic: When voters follow, or desert, a pre-electoral coalition
findings.claim: An experiment with Belgian students gave respondents either a party ballot or a coalition-cartel ballot. Whether supporters followed their party into a pre-electoral coalition depended on four factors: dislike of the partner, ideological congruence between the partners, the size of the voter's own party, and the pull of a specific high-profile candidate. Dislike of the partner operated independently of ideological distance. Loyalty to cartels grew over 2003-2005 as voters got used to them.
findings.quant: N = 1,255 students; four drivers identified; adjustment (rising loyalty) effect over 2003-2005.
findings.title: Should I stay or should I go? An experimental study on voter responses to pre-electoral coalitions
findings.relevance: Together (Bennett 2026 + Yesh Atid) is a pre-electoral coalition. Its leakage risk comes from voters who dislike the partner (right-leaning Bennett voters who dislike Lapid, and the reverse), not from ideology alone. A visible leader and shared candidates help hold them. The same logic applies to any declared change-bloc pact. Student sample: treat magnitudes as indicative.

findings.topic: When pre-electoral coalitions form, and whether commitments bind
findings.claim: Using all potential party pairs in 20 parliamentary democracies from 1946 to 1998, Golder finds that pre-electoral coalitions are more likely between ideologically similar parties of similar size, when the expected coalition is large but not too large, in polarised party systems, and under disproportional rules. Debus (2009, Public Choice 138:45-64, doi:10.1007/s11127-008-9338-2) finds that pre-electoral commitments significantly affect which governments form, even after controlling for endogeneity. The Debus finding is reported via secondary literature; its abstract was not retrieved.
findings.quant: 20 democracies, 1946-1998 (Golder). Debus: significant effect of commitments; magnitude not retrieved.
findings.title: Pre-Electoral Coalition Formation in Parliamentary Democracies; Pre-electoral commitments and government formation
findings.venue: British Journal of Political Science 36(2):193-212; Public Choice 138(1-2):45-64
findings.relevance: Israel's change bloc already acts as a loose pre-electoral coalition: three surplus pairs, a shared anti-Netanyahu identity and Together's joint list. Its public commitments will shape the post-election menu, so which commitments it makes is a strategic choice and not just rhetoric.

findings.topic: Blocs short of a majority can delay government formation
findings.claim: Using government formations in 17 West European democracies from 1945 to 2019, plus a case study of Sweden's long 2018-19 formation, the authors add commitment problems to the known causes of delay (preference uncertainty and bargaining complexity). Pre-electoral coalitions that fail to win a majority can delay government formation rather than speed it up. Lack of familiarity between parties can also make talks break down.
findings.quant: 17 countries, 1945-2019. In the Swedish case neither bloc had a majority and formation stalled; the paper's point is that bloc commitments short of a majority lengthen bargaining.
findings.authors: Hanna Bäck; Johan Hellström; Johannes Lindvall; Jan Teorell
findings.title: Pre-electoral coalitions, familiarity, and delays in government formation
findings.relevance: The 2026 forecast is the textbook case: a change bloc of about 51 and a Netanyahu bloc of about 55, both short. Rigid bloc pledges reproduce the 2019-21 stalemate (D10-F25). Commitments that leave a named cross-bloc option, such as unity without Netanyahu, are the comparative remedy. Prior cooperation between the parties (Bennett-Lapid 2021) is an asset.

findings.topic: Formateur advantage in portfolio allocation
findings.claim: Across coalition governments from 1946 to 2001, parties that join but do not form the government receive cabinet posts in linear proportion to their share of voting weight. The party that forms the government receives a substantial bonus over its voting weight. This fits proposal-power bargaining models: formateurs gain from agenda control, not from size.
findings.quant: Coalition governments 1946-2001. A substantial formateur bonus over voting weight; linear payoffs for non-formateur partners.
findings.authors: Stephen D. Ansolabehere; James M. Snyder Jr.; Aaron B. Strauss; Michael M. Ting
findings.title: Voting Weights and Formateur Advantages in the Formation of Coalition Governments
findings.relevance: The first mandate is worth fighting for even without a majority, because it controls the agenda and the calendar. Israel 2021 shows the reverse face of the same logic: a pivotal small list extracted the premiership (Bennett, 7 seats; D10-F26). The bloc should agree before the vote who receives everyone's recommendation.

findings.topic: Minority governments are a rational, common outcome
findings.claim: Minority cabinets made up roughly a third of governments in 15 parliamentary democracies after 1945. They are not explained by crisis, instability, polarisation or bargaining failure. They arise when opposition parties can still influence policy and when joining the cabinet is expected to cost a party votes at the next election.
findings.quant: About one-third of postwar governments in 15 democracies were minority cabinets.
findings.title: Minority Governments in Parliamentary Democracies: The Rationality of Nonwinning Cabinet Solutions
findings.relevance: This explains why Ra'am, the Joint List or the haredi parties may prefer outside support or abstention to cabinet seats: it gives them influence without the electoral cost of joining (see D10-F13). The bloc should design offers around policy influence (budgets, a crime plan, a draft framework) rather than ministries.

findings.topic: Minority governments with written support agreements last as long as majority governments
findings.claim: A survival analysis of 471 cabinets in 30 countries from 1977 to 2019 finds that minority status by itself does not make a government unstable. Minority cabinets without support agreements face a much higher risk of early termination than majority cabinets. Minority cabinets backed by written agreements with outside parties that secure a parliamentary majority are about as durable as majority cabinets.
findings.quant: 471 cabinets, 30 countries, 1977-2019. Minority cabinets with written support agreements are about as stable as majority cabinets; without agreements the hazard of early termination is much higher (exact hazard ratio not retrieved).
findings.title: Stability of minority governments and the role of support agreements
findings.relevance: If a change-led government depends on outside votes from Ra'am, the Joint List or abstaining haredi MKs, a public, written confidence-and-supply agreement that covers the budget is the single most stability-relevant design choice. Informal 'blocking' support (2019-20 style) is the fragile variant.

findings.topic: Junior coalition partners lose votes at the next election
findings.claim: Using data on 307 parties in 219 elections across 28 European countries from 1972 to 2017, the authors find that joining a cabinet as a junior partner considerably hurts a party's next election result. A case study points to two mechanisms: junior partners cannot deliver much of what they promised, and voters misperceive their record.
findings.quant: 307 parties, 219 elections, 28 countries, 1972-2017. A significant electoral penalty for junior partners.
findings.title: Helping or Hurting? How Governing as a Junior Coalition Partner Influences Electoral Outcomes
findings.relevance: Potential partners (Ra'am, Shas, UTJ, the Reservists, and YB and the Democrats inside the bloc) will price this cost in and demand visible, attributable wins. Israel fits the pattern: after 2021-22, the right-wing partners of the Bennett-Lapid government collapsed, while Ra'am, which could point to a large five-year budget plan (D10-F27), grew from 4 to 5 seats (D10-F26).

findings.topic: Voters punish parties they see as compromising
findings.claim: Survey data from six parliamentary democracies show that voters punish parties they perceive as compromising in coalition policy-making. Voters discount the achievements and promises of compromising parties. The effect is stronger among previous supporters of the incumbent cabinet and among the politically disinterested.
findings.quant: Six democracies. Perceived compromise lowers vote choice; effect strongest among prior cabinet supporters and low-interest voters.
findings.title: The Electoral Implications of Coalition Policy Making
findings.relevance: Absolute pre-election pledges that the arithmetic will probably force the bloc to break (for example 'never any Arab party in any form' when P(change alone >=61) is about 5%) set up the punishment mechanism. Conditional, policy-defined commitments are cheaper to keep. The Gantz (2020) and Yamina (2021) cases show the Israeli version (D10-F25, D10-F26).

findings.topic: Election frequency and voter fatigue
findings.claim: A natural experiment in the German state of Hesse compares municipalities that faced the same contest but different election frequencies because local elections were staggered. When two elections are held close together, turnout at the later one is significantly lower. The effect is stronger when voters see the election as less important.
findings.quant: Significant turnout reduction when elections are close together; larger for low-importance contests. Point estimate not retrieved.
findings.title: Election frequency, choice fatigue, and voter turnout
findings.relevance: A spring-2027 rerun (forecast probability about 42%) would follow within six months. Israeli national elections are high-salience, and the 2019-22 series did not show steady decline (68.5, 69.8, 71.5, 67.4, 70.6; D2-F02), so expect modest fatigue. Fatigue that differs by bloc matters more for seats than the national level.

findings.topic: Formation procedure and the 2026-27 calendar (Basic Law: The Government)
findings.claim: After consulting the parliamentary groups, the President assigns the task to an MK within 7 days of the published results, and that MK has 28 days, extendable by up to 14 (s.7-8). If the MK fails, the President has 3 days to task a second MK (28 days) or tell the Speaker no government is possible (s.9); a Knesset majority may then name an MK in writing within 21 days, who gets 14 days (s.10). Otherwise the Knesset is deemed dissolved and the election falls on the last Tuesday before day 90 (s.11). A dissolution law ends the process at any point (s.12).
findings.quant: Desk calculation, assuming official results on Wed 4 Nov 2026 (D+8): mandate by 11 Nov; 28 days to 9 Dec; with extension to 23 Dec; second MK to about 23 Jan 2027; 21-day window to about 13 Feb; election Tue 11 May 2027. Fast path (no second MK): election Tue 13 Apr 2027. Precedents from election to swearing-in: 58 days (2022) and 82 days (2021).
findings.authors: State of Israel (Knesset), unofficial English translation
findings.title: Basic Law: The Government (consolidated text, amendments through 15 August 2023)
findings.relevance: Gives the planning horizon. If any government forms, it would most likely be sworn in between late December 2026 and February 2027. A failure path leads to an April-May 2027 election, which needs field infrastructure kept alive through the winter. A Knesset dissolution law can short-circuit the calendar, as in May 2019.

findings.topic: The President's discretion: recommendations, not list size
findings.claim: The Basic Law sets no criteria for choosing whom to task. In practice the President weighs which candidate has the best chance, guided by how many MKs recommend each candidate and by list size, neither of which is binding. In February 2009 Kadima finished first (28 seats to Likud's 27), but President Peres tasked Netanyahu, who had 65 recommendations to Livni's 28. This departed from the custom of tasking the leader of the largest list.
findings.quant: 2009: Kadima 28 vs Likud 27 seats; recommendations Netanyahu 65, Livni 28; Labor, Meretz and the Arab parties recommended no one.
findings.authors: Ruth Levush (Library of Congress); Ynetnews staff
findings.title: Here We Go Again: Forming a Coalition Government Israeli-Style; Peres tasks Netanyahu with forming government
findings.venue: In Custodia Legis (Library of Congress blog); Ynetnews
findings.relevance: Yashar finishing first (or Likud finishing first) decides nothing by itself. The recommendation count is what matters, so the four change lists must agree in advance to recommend one candidate. Second source: https://www.ynetnews.com/article/3674886

findings.topic: Recommendation counts in the 2019-2021 deadlock
findings.claim: In September 2019 Netanyahu had 55 recommendations and Gantz 54, after Balad's 3 MKs withdrew from the Joint List's recommendation and Yisrael Beytenu recommended no one. Rivlin reportedly noted that 10 of Gantz's backers would not sit in a Gantz government, and he tasked Netanyahu first. In March 2020 parties with 61 MKs, including all Joint List factions (15 seats), recommended Gantz, but two Blue and White MKs (Hauser, Hendel) opposed a Joint List-backed government. In April 2021 the count was Netanyahu 52, Lapid 45, Bennett 7 and none 16, and Rivlin said no candidate had a realistic chance of forming a government.
findings.quant: Sept 2019: 55-54. March 2020: 61 for Gantz (Joint List 15 included). April 2021: 52/45/7/16 none.
findings.authors: Greer Fay Cashman (JPost); Globes staff; JNS staff
findings.title: Netanyahu 55, Gantz 54 as Rivlin concludes consultations; Majority of MKs recommend Gantz as prime minister; Israel's president (again) tasks Netanyahu
findings.relevance: Precedent cuts both ways for 2026. Arab-list recommendations can put a change candidate ahead (2020), but a President may discount recommenders who will not join the government (2019). A count that hangs on Joint List recommendations is weaker than one built on Zionist lists plus haredi abstention. Other URLs: https://en.globes.co.il/en/article-1001321919 and https://www.jns.org/israeli-president-tasks-netanyahu-with-forming-next-government

findings.topic: Rotation governments are legally enforceable
findings.claim: Since 2020 the Basic Law allows a 'rotation government' whose PM and Alternate PM, and the rotation date, are approved in the confidence vote (s.13a). Ministers are split by affiliation with parity in voting, and the PM cannot dismiss the Alternate PM or the Alternate's ministers (s.43c-43d). The PM cannot dissolve the Knesset without the Alternate's consent (s.43f), and neither of them may head a government formed by constructive no-confidence (s.43h). Amendment No. 10 (2021) adds that rotation happens early if the Knesset passes a dissolution law with at least two votes from the PM's side, or if the budget fails (s.43a1).
findings.quant: The early-rotation triggers: (1) a dissolution law backed by at least 2 MKs from the PM's side; (2) the budget-failure deadline. In 2022 these provisions made Lapid PM automatically when the Knesset dissolved.
findings.title: Basic Law: The Government, ss.5, 13a, 43a-43h (Amendments No. 8, 10, 11)
findings.relevance: This is the strongest credibility device available. A pre-election promise of rotation (Eisenkot-Bennett, or with a post-Netanyahu Likud leader) can be backed by a public commitment to legislate it under s.13a with the s.43a1 'poison pill'. That answers the reasonable objection, after Netanyahu-Gantz 2020, that rotation promises are worthless.

findings.topic: Constructive no-confidence: 61 votes for a named alternative
findings.claim: A government can be removed only by a Knesset majority (61) that simultaneously expresses confidence in an alternative government, with its policy guidelines, composition and distribution of portfolios (s.28). A partial version was adopted in 2001 and the full version in 2014, to prevent frequent toppling of governments. The Knesset can still dissolve itself by law with 61 votes.
findings.quant: 61 MKs are required, and the alternative government must be presented. A motion submitted by 61 MKs must be debated within a week.
findings.title: Constructive Motions of No-Confidence: Q&As
findings.relevance: Once sworn in, a change-led minority government cannot be brought down by the Netanyahu bloc unless that bloc assembles 61 for its own government. The realistic threats are a budget defeat and a dissolution law, not no-confidence. This lowers the risk of the minority option after investiture, not before it.

findings.topic: Investiture needs only a plurality; the budget is the real deadline
findings.claim: The government takes office once the Knesset 'expresses confidence' (s.13(d)); the Basic Law sets no special majority, and in practice a simple majority of those voting suffices. The Bennett-Lapid government was approved 60-59 with one Ra'am MK abstaining. Under Basic Law: The Knesset, the Knesset dissolves automatically if the budget is not passed by the end of March, or within 145 days of a new government's formation, with elections about three months later. This rule has been triggered once, in December 2020 (after a 120-day extension).
findings.quant: Investiture 60-59-1 (13 June 2021). Budget deadline: 31 March or 145 days after formation. Triggered once (23rd Knesset, Dec 2020).
findings.title: Israel's State Budget is Directly Linked to Dissolution of Knesset and Elections
findings.relevance: Abstentions from Ra'am, the Joint List or a haredi faction can install a government without anyone formally joining it. Its survival then hinges on passing a 2027 budget within 145 days. Any support agreement must name the budget explicitly (D10-F12).

findings.topic: Early dissolution is the Israeli norm
findings.claim: Only 6 of the first 23 Knessets served a full term; the other 17 were dissolved early. The 22nd Knesset's 21-day window under s.10 lapsed on the night of 11-12 December 2019, and the Knesset passed a dissolution law the same day. After the April 2019 election, the 21st Knesset dissolved itself (29-30 May 2019) before any government had been formed.
findings.quant: 6/23 full terms; budget-failure dissolution once (2020); PM-order dissolution once (2005).
findings.title: Dissolving the Knesset: A Historical Survey
findings.relevance: The base rate for short-lived Knessets is high. Any change-led government should be planned as a 12-24 month project with a priority legislative list (budget, inquiry commission, draft law), not a four-year term. Note that the 25th Knesset ran close to full term, so 2026 opens a new cycle.

findings.topic: Rabin 1992-95: outside support from Arab parties
findings.claim: In 1992 Labor (44), Meretz (12), Hadash (3) and the Arab Democratic Party (2) formed a 61-seat blocking bloc, but Rabin kept the Arab parties out of the government and formed a 62-seat coalition with Shas, with the 5 Arab MKs supporting from outside. Deri resigned in September 1993 and Shas stayed out until 1996, leaving a 56-MK government that survived because Hadash and the Arab Democratic Party blocked no-confidence motions. Oslo I passed 61-50 with 8 abstentions (Shas abstained), and Oslo II reportedly passed 61-59 in October 1995 with the votes of Tzomet defectors.
findings.quant: Coalition 62 + 5 outside; 56 MKs after September 1993; Oslo I 61-50-8 (23 Sept 1993); Oslo II 61-59 (reported). Turnout 77.4%.
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute; Ron Gerlitz (+972 Magazine); Peter Ford (Christian Science Monitor)
findings.title: 1992 elections (IDI); Rabin's legacy: a government inclusive of all citizens; Israel's Parliament Votes 'Yes' on Peace Plan
findings.relevance: This is the only multi-year Israeli precedent for a centre-led minority government sustained by Arab parties from outside. It shows the model can last about two years and pass major legislation. The +972 account is an opinion piece, so the 56-MK figure is medium confidence. Other URLs: https://www.972mag.com/rabins-legacy-a-government-inclusive-of-all-citizens-not-only-jews/ and https://proof.csmonitor.com/1993/0924/24022.html

findings.topic: Unity governments, 1984-1990
findings.claim: In 1984 the Alignment (44) and Likud (41) were deadlocked and formed a national unity government with a rotating premiership: Peres served two years, then Shamir. It had 25 ministers and was the largest government up to then. In 1988 (Likud 40, Alignment 39) Shamir formed another unity government without rotation. It ended in March 1990 when the Alignment joined a no-confidence vote, and in June 1990 Shamir formed a narrow right-religious government.
findings.quant: 1984: 44 vs 41 seats; 2-year rotation honoured. 1988: 40 vs 39; unity ended March 1990 by no-confidence; narrow government June 1990.
findings.title: 1984 elections; 1988 elections
findings.relevance: Unity has been Israel's way out of big-party near-ties: in 1984 it ended a real deadlock, and in 1988 Shamir chose it even though a narrow right-religious majority existed. In a different form it was used again in 2020. Rotation was honoured in 1984 without legal force, through the political cost of reneging. In 2020 it was not honoured (D10-F25), and that failure led to the 2021 legal fix (D10-F19). See also https://en.idi.org.il/israeli-elections-and-parties/elections/1988/

findings.topic: 2019-2021: what caused the deadlock and what broke it
findings.claim: After April 2019 Netanyahu failed to form a government because Liberman refused any compromise on the haredi draft law, and the Knesset dissolved itself first; after September 2019 neither Netanyahu (55) nor Gantz (54) formed one and the 21-day window lapsed. In March 2020 Gantz held 61 recommendations but split his alliance and entered a legally entrenched rotation government under Netanyahu, ending 18 months of deadlock. That government fell when the budget failed in December 2020, and the rotation never happened. The deadlock was broken by a centre faction defecting (2020) and by a kingmaker premiership plus an Arab party entering (2021), never by a haredi party switching sides.
findings.quant: Four elections, April 2019 to March 2021. Later results: Gantz's Blue and White 8 seats (2021; it had 33 as the joint list in 2020, a figure not re-verified in this pass). Yisrael Beytenu rose from 5 to 8 seats between the two 2019 elections, so the party blamed for the repeat was not punished (official results, not re-fetched).
findings.title: 2019 elections; 2020 elections; 2021 elections (IDI election pages)
findings.relevance: These are the base rates for 2026's 42% repeat-election branch. Deadlocks persisted while both blocs held firm, and they broke through pledge-breaking or kingmaker deals. A party that holds a popular red line (Liberman on the draft) can gain in a rerun, while a party that breaks a red line loses heavily (Gantz). See also https://en.idi.org.il/israeli-elections-and-parties/elections/2021/

findings.topic: Bennett-Lapid 2021-22: Ra'am inside, kingmaker PM, rotation clause
findings.claim: In 2021 the Netanyahu bloc won 52 seats, and Yair Lapid (Yesh Atid, 17) assembled an eight-party coalition in which Naftali Bennett (Yamina, 7 seats) became PM under a legally entrenched rotation. Ra'am (4 seats) became the first independent Arab party in decades to join a governing coalition. The government won confidence 60-59-1, lost its majority through defections, and the Knesset dissolved on 30 June 2022, at which point Lapid automatically became PM. In 2022 Ra'am rose to 5 seats (4.1%), while Jewish Home (1.2%), Meretz (3.2%) and Balad (2.9%) fell below the threshold.
findings.quant: 2021: NB 52; Yamina 7 gets PM; Ra'am 4. Investiture 60-59-1 (reported). 2022: Ra'am 5 seats (4.1%); Jewish Home 1.2%; Meretz 3.2%. About 10% of 2021 coalition voters planned to move to the NB (D1-F10).
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute; Times of Israel (reporting)
findings.title: 2021 elections; 2022 elections (IDI election pages)
findings.relevance: Proof of concept for a change government with Ra'am inside. The electoral cost fell on its right-wing Jewish partners, not on Ra'am. The government lasted about a year because it had no margin: a 61-seat coalition dies with one defector. A larger or formally supported arrangement is needed for durability.

findings.topic: What Ra'am got: the five-year plan for Arab society (Resolution 550)
findings.claim: Government Resolution 550 (October 2021) set a five-year economic plan for Arab society for 2022-2026, worth about NIS 30 billion, more than double its predecessor (Resolution 922). The 2024 revised budget cut it substantially, and further 2026 reductions were adopted (Decision 4387, July 2026, as summarised; not fetched). The plan expires at the end of 2026.
findings.quant: About NIS 30 bn over 2022-2026 (Bank of Israel description). The plan expires 31 Dec 2026. Full official text not fetched (gov.il returned 403).
findings.authors: Government of Israel; Bank of Israel (summary)
findings.title: Government Resolution 550: Economic plan to reduce gaps in Arab society, 2022-2026
findings.relevance: A successor plan, together with the crime emergency (D5-F01, D5-F02), is the natural policy content of any 2026-27 support agreement with Ra'am or the Joint List. It is a budget item that can be written into the budget the government must pass within 145 days (D10-F21). Whether to offer it is a leadership decision.

findings.topic: Haredi parties' coalition record: transactional and pivot-dependent
findings.claim: Shas joined Rabin's government in 1992 and Barak's in 1999 (with four portfolios), leaving the first in 1993 after Deri's indictment and the second over disputes with Meretz and Camp David. It stayed out in 2003 (refusing to sit with Shinui) and in 2013-15. In July 2025 UTJ quit Netanyahu's government over the draft-exemption law and Shas ministers resigned; AP reported the government reduced to a 50-seat minority. Shas nonetheless stayed formally in the coalition, said it would not help topple the government, and kept seats on committees and in the kitchen cabinet.
findings.quant: Shas in non-Likud governments: 1992-93, 1999-2000. Opposition: 1993-96, 2003, 2013-15. July 2025: 67-seat majority reduced to 50 seats after the haredi exits (reported).
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute; PBS NewsHour / AP; JNS (reporting)
findings.title: Shas (party page); Another Netanyahu ally quits governing coalition, leaving Israeli leader with minority in parliament
findings.relevance: Haredi parties exit over the draft and yeshiva funding but avoid toppling governments. They have crossed to non-Likud governments only when pivotal and when the right had no path (the 1992 precedent; UTJ's brief 1999 participation is per the formation-model dossier, not re-verified). For 2026, that makes abstention or tolerance more plausible than joining. See also https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/another-netanyahu-ally-quits-governing-coalition-leaving-israeli-leader-with-minority-in-parliament

findings.topic: Haredi parties' reported 2026 plan: recommend nobody, sit out a year
findings.claim: Citing Maariv, the Jerusalem Post (17 Sept 2026) reports that Shas and UTJ lean toward recommending neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot. They would sit in opposition for about a year so that the next government passes a draft law without their signatures, and could then consider joining, including an Eisenkot-led government. Eisenkot has made mandatory service a core condition and reportedly prefers another election to compromising on it. Both sides deny any contacts, and sources doubt Shas would join without UTJ.
findings.quant: Yeshiva and institutions funding at stake: NIS 1.2-1.4 bn, at most about NIS 1.5 bn (sources). The account describes a mood, not a formal decision.
findings.authors: Anna Barsky (The Jerusalem Post, citing Maariv)
findings.title: Haredi parties preparing for shift in political strategy for 2026 elections
findings.relevance: If carried out, this changes the formation game. Netanyahu's recommendations fall to about 39-43, which makes a change candidate's first mandate plausible (D10-F32). Haredi outside tolerance could also lower the investiture bar. The price, a draft law the haredim can criticise but live with plus funding, can be planned for now. Low-cost pre-election signal: the draft as a universal policy test, not a ban on parties.

findings.topic: Kingmaker lists' stated 2026 conditions (Reservists, Amcha)
findings.claim: Reservists-Economic leader Yoaz Hendel (23 Aug 2026) wants a 'Zionist government' only: he will not complete a 61-seat majority with haredi parties or be the 61st seat of an opposition government that depends on Arab parties, and he says Netanyahu should go. On 8 Oct he urged Ofer Winter (Amcha) to form a joint 'blocking bloc' against coalitions with haredi or Arab parties; no deal was reported, and in the same report Otzma accused Likud of seeking a unity government with Eisenkot. Winter (2 Sept) will recommend Netanyahu but will join only if a national-service law passes before the government is sworn in.
findings.quant: Forecast pass probabilities: Reservists about 0.20, Amcha about 0.15. Their stated conditions fit only a pure-Zionist change coalition or a unity government.
findings.authors: JPost staff (103FM interview); Keshet Neev (JPost); Israel National News staff
findings.title: Yoaz Hendel rules out coalition with haredi or Arab parties; Hendel calls on Ofer Winter to break with Netanyahu's bloc; Winter's condition for Netanyahu
findings.venue: The Jerusalem Post; Israel National News
findings.relevance: If either list passes, its seats count toward a change government only in the unity or Zionist-only branches. Rescuing their voters (MODEL_BRIEF rescue lever) helps change formation less than it helps denying Netanyahu 61. Unity talk is already in the public debate (Otzma's charge), which lowers the cost of the bloc stating it. Other URLs: https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-911020 and https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/432614

findings.topic: Other 2026 signals on record in the formation model (unverified in this pass)
findings.claim: The formation model's notes record further 2026 signals: Eisenkot has called a 58-59-seat minority government acceptable (ToI, 23 Aug), Liberman says 'no minority government, no safety net' (N12), and every Jewish change list pledges no Arab party inside at the outset. Eisenkot's camp published Ra'am-shaped entry conditions (Walla, 16 Aug), Ra'am's Shura council veto was abolished in December 2025, Ra'am runs a joint slate with a former Yesh Atid MK (Segalovitz), and President Herzog is reported to be pushing for a unity outcome. None of these were re-fetched in this pass because the shared web-search budget ran out.
findings.quant: No new numbers; qualitative positions only.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model formation desk (internal notes citing ToI, N12, Walla, Haaretz, NYT/JNS)
findings.title: src/government_formation.py BEHAVIOR notes; docs/priors_dossier.md
findings.relevance: Together with D10-F29 and D10-F30, these define the 2026 bargaining space. The Eisenkot-minority and Liberman-veto tension is the key internal inconsistency the bloc must settle before election day if it wants the minority branch to be credible. Re-verify each item against the primary article before it goes into the guide.

findings.topic: Forecast arithmetic: what each signal opens or closes
findings.claim: With the change lists at about 51 seats, the Netanyahu core at about 55 (with Shas and UTJ) and the Arab lists at about 14, P(change alone >=61) is 5.2%, P(change + Ra'am >=61) is 18.8% and P(NB >=61) is 21.7%. The formation model gives a change-led government about 18% and a repeat election about 42%. On the forecast medians, recommendations would be Netanyahu about 39 (Likud+Otzma+RZP), plus 16 if Shas and UTJ recommend him, against about 51 for a single change candidate, plus 14 if both Arab lists recommend. Arab-list votes help deny Netanyahu 61 but are neutral (Ra'am, -0.08) or negative (Joint List, -0.48 net-vote equivalents per vote) for a change-led government in the model's exchange rates.
findings.quant: P(change alone >=61) 5.2%; with Ra'am 18.8%; P(NB >=61) 21.7%; P(change-led) 18.2-18.5%; repeat 41.9%. Recommendation scenarios: 51 vs 39 (haredim recommend nobody); 51 vs 55 (haredim recommend Netanyahu); 65 vs 55 (Arab lists also recommend the change candidate).
findings.title: MODEL_BRIEF v3 for content writers (forecast of 10 Oct 2026)
findings.relevance: Without Ra'am, a haredi party or Likud-without-Netanyahu, the bloc's route to government is about 5%. Pledges should therefore close options cheaply for voters (no Arab party ministers, no draft exemption) but not close the outside-support or unity routes. The first mandate is within reach only if all four lists recommend the same candidate and the haredim abstain from recommending.

parameters.name: coalition_motivated_vote_share
parameters.value: About 10% of voters cast a coalition-motivated (non-favourite) vote; responsiveness to new signals is concentrated among mainstream-list voters
parameters.basis: P-F27 (about 1 in 10, Israel 2003); D1-F24 (effect for main parties only); D10-F01, D10-F02, D10-F03 (common but small strategic core).

parameters.name: pm_candidate_signal_effect
parameters.value: A joint four-list declaration of one PM candidate: about 0 net change-bloc seats; shifts about 1-2 seats toward the named candidate's list from the other change lists
parameters.range: Net bloc -0.5 to +0.5 seats; intra-bloc shift 0.5-3 seats
parameters.basis: D1-F25 (formateur optimisation, stronger when the race between formateurs is close); D10-F04, D10-F05 (signals raise coalition weight; ambiguity costs); P-F17 (volatility mainly intra-bloc). Judgment, not an estimated coefficient.

parameters.name: p_first_mandate_change_candidate
parameters.value: 0.55 if Shas and UTJ recommend no one and all four change lists recommend one candidate; 0.15 if the haredim recommend Netanyahu
parameters.basis: D10-F17, D10-F18 (President follows recommendation counts; 2019 discount for recommenders who won't sit); D10-F29 (reported haredi plan); D10-F32 (51 vs about 39). Judgment.

parameters.name: formation_duration_if_success_days
parameters.value: About 70 days from election to swearing-in (early-mid January 2027)
parameters.basis: D10-F16 (statutory clock, 2022 = 58 days, 2021 = 82 days); D10-F09 (blocs short of a majority lengthen bargaining).

parameters.name: repeat_election_date_window
parameters.value: Tue 11 May 2027 if all statutory stages are used; Tue 13 Apr 2027 if no second MK is tasked
parameters.range: Earlier if the new Knesset passes a dissolution law (May 2019 precedent)
parameters.basis: D10-F16 (ss.7-12; desk calculation assuming results on 4 Nov 2026); D10-F22 (self-dissolution precedent).

parameters.name: minority_government_survival_adjustment
parameters.value: Treat a minority change government with a written, public support agreement covering the budget as majority-equivalent for survival; without one, apply a substantially higher early-termination hazard (judgment: roughly double)
parameters.range: Hazard multiplier 1.0 (with agreement) to 2-3 (without); multiplier is judgment, the direction is from the data
parameters.basis: D10-F12 (471 cabinets); D10-F11; D10-F21 (145-day budget test); D10-F23 (Rabin 1993-95).

parameters.name: likud_sans_bibi (formation model)
parameters.basis: D10-F24 (unity ended the 1984 deadlock; chosen again in 1988 despite a 65-seat right-religious bloc); D10-F25 (2020 unity via a centre pledge-break, not via Likud dropping Netanyahu); D10-F09; D10-F30 (unity already in public debate).

parameters.name: shas_defects / utj_defects (immediate, at formation)
parameters.value: Shas 0.08, UTJ 0.10 for joining at formation; add a separate haredi tolerance (abstain on investiture or budget) channel at 0.15 conditional on a draft law being in train
parameters.basis: D10-F28 (joined non-Likud governments only when pivotal; exit without toppling in 2025); D10-F29 (reported plan to sit out about a year); D10-F11 (outside support is rational). Values are desk judgment, set slightly below the model's current 0.10/0.15 because of the reported sit-out plan.

parameters.name: centre_defects (pledge-break to a Netanyahu government)
parameters.basis: D10-F25 (Gantz 2020: 1 of 3 feasible deadlocks); D10-F13, D10-F14 (electoral cost of compromise; Blue and White fell to 8 seats in 2021).

parameters.name: liberman_minority_ok
parameters.basis: D10-F18 (March 2020: Yisrael Beytenu among the 61 recommending Gantz alongside the Joint List, reported); D10-F31 (stated veto, unverified this pass).

parameters.name: repeat_election_turnout_shift
parameters.value: -1.0 pp national turnout in a spring-2027 rerun versus Oct 2026
parameters.basis: D10-F15 (fatigue when elections are close together; weaker for high-salience contests); D2-F02 (Israeli series 2019-2022: +1.3, +1.7, -4.1, +3.2 pp).

open_questions: The shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so several 2026 items in D10-F31 could not be re-checked against primary articles: Eisenkot's minority-government remarks, Liberman's 'no safety net' veto, Ra'am's Shura change and Segalovitz slot, and Herzog's unity push.

No Israeli experiment tests specific 2026 coalition signals (Ra'am inside vs outside, unity without Netanyahu, haredi tolerance) on vote choice. A vignette module in a private tracking poll (private polling remains allowed during the 24-27 Oct publication blackout) would give the only direct estimate.

Will Herzog count recommendations from lists that will not sit in the government (the September 2019 discount) if the Joint List or Ra'am recommend Eisenkot? The President's office has published no criteria.
Will Shas and UTJ formally decide to recommend no one (Council of Torah Sages) and abstain on investiture, or only stay out of a government? Track this after 27 Oct.

Effect sizes were not retrieved for Bahnsen-Stoetzer-Gschwend (2025), Gschwend-Meffert-Stoetzer (2017), Debus (2009) or Krauss-Thürk (2022) hazard ratios. Martin & Stevenson (2001, AJPS 45(1):33-50) on pre-electoral pacts and 'anti-pacts' could not be verified, so it is not cited.

Are the 2021 rotation triggers (s.43a1) and other rotation provisions unchanged since August 2023? The English translation is current only to that date. Check against the Hebrew National Legislation Database.

How do the budget rules interact with a formation that runs past 1 January 2027 (continuation budget; the 31 March vs 145-day deadline)? This needs a Knesset legal-adviser reading for minority-government planning.

No peer-reviewed analysis of Ra'am's 2021-22 coalition record or Rabin's 1993-95 minority government was found in this pass. The Dayan Center (Bayan) one-year assessment timed out. Current sources are IDI pages and reporting.
